questions.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y={e}^{2x}.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}+4{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-4x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{-4x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{-4x})}^{′}+4(u{e}^{-4x}) & ={e}^{2x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-4x}-4u{e}^{-4x}+4u{e}^{-4x} & ={e}^{2x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-4x}-\cancel{4u{e}^{-4x}}+\cancel{4u{e}^{-4x}} & ={e}^{2x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-4x} & ={e}^{2x} \\ {u}^{′} & ={e}^{6x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & ={e}^{6x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{6x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =\frac{1}{6}{e}^{6x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{-4x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{-4x} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{e}^{6x}\cdot {e}^{-4x} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-4y={e}^{4x}.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-4{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{4x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{4x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{4x})}^{′}-4(u{e}^{4x}) & ={e}^{4x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{4x}+4u{e}^{4x}-4u{e}^{4x} & ={e}^{4x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{4x}+\cancel{4u{e}^{4x}}-\cancel{4u{e}^{4x}} & ={e}^{4x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{4x} & ={e}^{4x} \\ {u}^{′} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =1 \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ u & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{4x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{4x} \\  & =x{e}^{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y=7.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}+4{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-4x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{-4x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{-4x})}^{′}+4(u{e}^{-4x}) & =7 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-4x}-4u{e}^{-4x}+4u{e}^{-4x} & =7 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-4x}-\cancel{4u{e}^{-4x}}+\cancel{4u{e}^{-4x}} & =7 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-4x} & =7 \\ {u}^{′} & =7{e}^{4x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =7{e}^{4x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 7{e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =\frac{7}{4}{e}^{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{-4x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{-4x} \\  & =\frac{7}{4}{e}^{4x}\cdot {e}^{-4x} \\  & =\frac{7}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-4y=12\operatorname{cosh}⁡4x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-4{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{4x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{4x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{4x})}^{′}-4(u{e}^{4x}) & =12\operatorname{cosh}⁡4x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{4x}+4u{e}^{4x}-4u{e}^{4x} & =12\operatorname{cosh}⁡4x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{4x}+\cancel{4u{e}^{4x}}-\cancel{4u{e}^{4x}} & =12\operatorname{cosh}⁡4x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{4x} & =12\operatorname{cosh}⁡4x \\ {u}^{′} & =12{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cosh}⁡4x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡4x=\frac{{e}^{4x}+{e}^{-4x}}{2}
$$

our equation for $u$ becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =12{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cosh}⁡4x \\  & =12{e}^{-4x}(\frac{{e}^{4x}+{e}^{-4x}}{2}) \\  & =6{e}^{-4x}({e}^{4x}+{e}^{-4x}) \\  & =6+6{e}^{-8x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =6+6{e}^{-8x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 6+6{e}^{-8x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =6x-\frac{3}{4}{e}^{-8x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{4x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{4x} \\  & =6x{e}^{4x}-\frac{3}{4}{e}^{-4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y={e}^{2x}.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-3{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{3x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{3x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{3x})}^{′}-3(u{e}^{3x}) & ={e}^{2x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+3u{e}^{3x}-3u{e}^{3x} & ={e}^{2x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}}-\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}} & ={e}^{2x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x} & ={e}^{2x} \\ {u}^{′} & ={e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & ={e}^{-x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =-{e}^{-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{3x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{3x} \\  & =-{e}^{-x}\cdot {e}^{3x} \\  & =-{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the first-order linear ODE dydx−3y=e2x. We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form
u(x)e3x
u(x)e3x
u(x)e−3x
u(x)e2x
u(x)e−2x
u(x)e−x
.

Solving for u, we have u(x)=
−e−x
−e−x
e−x
−ex
ex
−e2x
.

Therefore, the particular solution is yp(x)=
−e2x
−e2x
e2x
−ex
e3x
e−x
.
